brief.head: No cluster by decree
brief.text: Clusters matter, Ajay Shah said, but they emerge organically, as in Tirupur’s garments and Gujarat’s chemicals. “It is not true that you can will these into existence.” {089-C03}

brief.head: Lobby, don’t compete
brief.text: Decades of a protected economy taught Indian firms to get ahead by working the state, Amit Varma said: too often an Indian entrepreneur asks how to influence a joint secretary. {089-C12}

brief.head: Method over machine
brief.text: To an engineer a technology is a machine, Ajay Shah said; to an economist it is technique. Productivity lives in know-how, learned by doing. {089-C15}

brief.head: Growth is the defence
brief.text: The army should solve the problem of Chinese backdoors for itself, Ajay Shah said, not turn the whole economy against foreigners. Strength comes from 8 per cent growth. {089-C18}

brief.head: Unhappy in its own way
brief.text: China’s EVs and solar panels are cherry-picked successes, Ajay Shah said. In the round, “all successful advanced economies look alike. All unhappy, poor countries are unhappy in their own way.” {089-C19}

thought.who: Ajay Shah, on why many private long shots beat one government champion

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on states that pick winners
lead.head: Don’t pick winners, enable them
body: A fan wrote to Amit Varma to say that he and Ajay Shah were so smart they should plan India’s economy. Varma found those last lines deeply disturbing. {089-S01}
You can plan your own day, he replied, but not a country. “Planning a country is just a conception of great hubris,” Varma said. “Our hero Friedrich Hayek called it the fatal conceit.” {089-C01}
Industrial policy, he said, is a classic case of that top-down thinking, and should not be done better. It should not be done at all.

Shah had learnt humility the hard way. As a “callow” 35-year-old hired into the Ministry of Finance by Yashwant Sinha, he found within days that the job was truly hard, and that “there are no obvious mistakes”. {089-S02}
## Four ways to pick a winner
Industrial policy, Shah said, is “the game of a government that picks winners”: this industry, technology, firm or place of production is good, that one bad. {089-C02}
The state has four levers for it: subsidies, coercive power, ethno-nationalism and outright monopoly. With the first, Varma observed, it plays venture capitalist; with the last, entrepreneur.
Shah’s premise was arithmetic. GDP is the sum of the value added by firms, so “the story of economic development is centrally a story of firms”, and of the incentives they face. {089-C04}
Subsidies, he argued, put the state in place of finance. Finance places many long shots, most of which fail; a government backs one champion through thick and thin. {089-C06}

Public money is dearer still. People and firms reorganise their lives to dodge tax, and pay lawyers and accountants besides. “It turns out that the marginal cost of public funds is three,” Shah said. {#mcpf}
Varma went further: every intervention in free markets, he said, “amounts to a redistribution of wealth from the poor to the rich”. {089-C08}
## Patches and protection

The government’s production-linked incentives, or PLI, compensate firms such as Apple for mistakes in India’s indirect taxes. Shah agreed that Apple deserved it, but wanted the tax system fixed at the root, so that thousands of other global firms would come too. {089-C13}

Protection fails twice over, Varma argued. A tariff on a better foreign rival hurts consumers, and spares the Indian firm the need to improve. “You’re hurting the consumer and you’re hurting the Indian company.” {089-C17}

The fourth lever is the bluntest. Air India began as a Tata company, was taken over by the government and made a monopoly, turned into a zombie firm living on public money, and was finally sold back to the Tatas.
## The state’s real job

The job of policy, Shah said, “is to enable winners, not pick winners”: fund research in an industry-neutral way, keep competition fierce from start-up to bankruptcy, open the economy to trade and foreign firms, and welcome immigrants. {089-C20}
Varma added a caution: most monopolies exist only with the state’s collusion, so its job is chiefly the rule of law.

Shah closed with SEEPZ, a walled zone set up in north Bombay in the 1970s so that radios could be made for export. The industries that flourished there were two that no planner foresaw: diamond polishing and computer software.
“You can’t predict, you can’t control,” Shah said, “but adding freedom is always a good thing.” {089-S08}

second.label: Capital controls
second.head: Chickens get the credit
second.deck: The RBI once let nine industries borrow abroad. Ajay Shah read the list
body: The Reserve Bank of India has long policed borrowing from abroad, and Ajay Shah has never seen an economic reason for it. One day a rule said external commercial borrowing would be allowed for nine industries only. {#nine}

Those chosen would get cheaper foreign credit; the rest would not. Shah, “bloody minded and masochistic” enough to read such documents, found that the list included nanotechnology and poultry farms. “Amit, you’re not eating enough chicken,” he said. {089-S04}
Amit Varma foresaw “really tiny chickens”. Ask at a poultry farm for the subsidised bird, he said, and you will be told: “we have nano chickens.” {089-J04}

quote.text: Chicken needs cheap credit. So we will give exclusive access to external commercial borrowing to poultry farms.

second.caption: the RBI’s chosen industries

third.head: Indians export, not India
body: Ajay Shah was the junior-most person in the room at a Ministry of Finance meeting run by Ashok Lahiri, then chief economic advisor. On the routine agenda: the Ministry of Commerce setting a target for India’s exports. {089-S03}
Shah asked what the Ministry of Commerce, or any of them, had to do with what India exports. “India is a collection of people, and those people export,” he said.

Exporting decisions are made by individual firms, he argued. The state can create enabling conditions; what exports actually materialise happens in society, and is not for a government to plan, control or set a target for.
Even the word target, Shah said, is “semi-offensive”: miss it, and an urgent mid-year meeting is called to think up “policy measures to boost exports”. {#target}
third.caption: the export target

p2.title: The four levers
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s anatomy of industrial policy, lever by lever, and what the state should do instead {089-C02}

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: A ministry for every trade
sections.caption: what industrial policy is
body: Industrial policy, Ajay Shah said, is the game of a government that picks winners. Officials decide which industry, technology, firm or place of production is good and which is bad. When such decisions are placed in the hands of the government, “it’s called industrial policy”. {089-C02}
Growing up in India, he said, you see the whole firmament: ministries of industry, textiles, chemicals, steel and IT, and special attention for handlooms.
## Grown, not declared

Clusters show where the line is crossed. Silicon Valley, Tirupur’s garments and Gujarat’s chemicals grew organically, as skills, vendors and labour markets gathered. Governments see them and try to declare their own, Shah said, and the choice gets contaminated by “equity”, every state wanting one, or by a powerful politician’s constituency. {089-C03}

Behind this lies his central claim. GDP is the sum of the value added by firms, and rich countries are full of high-productivity firms. People are the same everywhere: Sundar Pichai and Satya Nadella are Indians. What differs is the incentives of the operating environment. {089-C04}

~ Amit Varma put it his own way: growth happens through firms, as entrepreneurs scramble to fulfil each other’s needs, and the government’s job is to provide a rule of law under which they compete without coercion.

quote.text: Indians are not inferior. Sundar Pichai is an Indian. Satya Nadella is an Indian. So there’s nothing wrong with Indians.

sections.label: Lever one
sections.head: The rupee that costs three
sections.caption: subsidies and public money
body: A subsidy can be a tax break, a cheap input or cash, Ajay Shah said, but it always boils down to public money. His first question was why a government should do what finance already does: if poultry farms are a great investment, buy their shares or lend to them.

If Indian finance works poorly, he said, the fix is to repair it and let foreign financial firms in. Finance hunts all day for the next good opportunity, placing dozens of long shots, most of which fail, while a government backs one national champion through thick and thin. {089-C06}
Shah reached for Oliver Cromwell: “in the bowels of Christ, consider it possible you may be mistaken.” {089-J17}
## Blood money

Public money, he said, is “coerced out of the people”. People reorganise their lives to avoid tax, and the economy carries lawyers, accounts departments and jails. Each rupee spent costs about three in GDP, which defence or a vaccination campaign can justify, and poultry farms cannot. {089-C07}

~ Amit Varma added Milton Friedman’s matrix. Spend your own money on yourself and you both economise and seek value. The government spends somebody else’s money on somebody else, and does neither. {089-C09}

quote.text: Public money is coerced out of the people. Taxation has blood on it.

sections.label: The folly of PLI
sections.head: Paying back what tax took
sections.caption: production-linked incentives
body: Production-linked incentives, or PLI, are the government’s new effort at paying subsidies explicitly to some industries. Export subsidies break WTO rules, Ajay Shah explained, so the payments are tied to production.
Shah called Apple’s presence in India a great achievement, one that could push local vendors from hundred-micron errors to one-micron ones.
## Small errors, big swings

Ila Patnaik, he said, taught him how much small tax mistakes matter. The profit after tax of the average non-financial Indian firm is 6 per cent of sales, so an indirect-tax error of 1 to 3 per cent can swing its return on equity hugely. {#pat}
Good countries refund indirect taxes to exporters, because you do not tax foreigners. India does not, so Apple is right to ask for compensation, and PLI provides it. {089-C13}

But only giants can afford what Shah described as a $10 million operation in Delhi, to negotiate with government and actually get paid. {#tenmn} Fix the tax system at the root, he said, and thousands of global firms would do more in India.

~ Other “disabilities”, such as costly transport, erratic electricity or unskilled workers, deserve not a shred of attention, he added. With some of the world’s lowest wages, firms in India have “a huge sort of negative disability” in their pocket. {089-C14}

quote.text: PLI is a reversal of inappropriate taxation. A simple dharma of public finance is you don’t tax non-residents.

sections.label: Lever two
sections.head: A camera doesn’t make Nomsita
sections.caption: coercion and technology
body: Coercion is the lever Amit Varma hates most, and Ajay Shah explained why it spreads. Spending is reined in by a budget that has to add up. “There’s no budget constraint of coercive power,” he said. {089-C05}

When the state backs one technology, as with income tax inspectors who can fine shops that refuse UPI, it assumes it knows best. Nobody in government can survey the world’s complexity and choose, Shah said. Multiple rival standards battling for supremacy are a healthy thing.
## Machines and know-how
Those who push a technology think productivity lives in the machine. To an engineer, Shah said, technology is a machine; to an economist, it is everything about technique. {089-C15}
Give an army great tanks and it does not become world class. And if any idiot had a Sony Alpha camera, he said, “they do not become Nomsita”, who shoots the show. {089-J06}
Know-how is learned by doing, and it travels through people, such as alumni of Hindustan Lever who carried Unilever’s knowledge into new consumer goods companies.
~ Varma added that technology never stands still, and that you have to be at the cutting edge of the ecosystem to really understand it.

quote.text: To an engineer, a technology is a machine. To an economist, technology is everything about technique.

sections.label: Lever three
sections.head: The firm that never grows up
sections.caption: protection and foreign firms
body: The third lever, ethno-nationalism, favours Indian firms and keeps foreigners out. Ajay Shah could not imagine the universe in which it works. How will you ever make Indian firms better, he asked, by reducing the competitive pressure on them from global firms?
The state of the art lives inside foreign firms, so their presence spreads know-how across India. “If anything you want it upside down,” he said. “You want more foreign firms here.” {089-C16}
Even “Indian firm” is slippery: ICICI Bank is 90 per cent owned by foreigners, and Microsoft has an Indian CEO. {#icici}
## Seen and unseen

Amit Varma set out protectionism’s two unseen effects. When a tariff shields Indian firm A from a better Italian firm X, the seen effect is that A prospers. Unseen, consumers lose lower prices or better value, and A, spared the world’s best, stays stuck in a low equilibrium. {089-C17}

National security is a real exception, Shah said: the army should keep Chinese backdoors out of its gear through trusted supply chains and partners. That is no reason to distort the whole economy. {089-C18}
~ Russia, he noted, has an Italy-sized GDP, which is why Europe can absorb the threat. {089-J09} Varma said many Italian viewers were at this point deeply disappointed.

quote.text: So you’re not even helping the Indian company. You’re hurting the consumer and you’re hurting the Indian company.

sections.label: The alternative
sections.head: Make life hard for firms
sections.caption: what the state should do
body: Asked what he would do if he did run the country, Ajay Shah offered a phrase: the job of policy is “to enable winners, not pick winners”. Geniuses are hiding in the private sector, and nobody knows who or where they are. {089-C20}

First comes research, contracted out to universities and private firms in an industry-neutral way. He would challenge firms to land a craft on Venus, “a nonsensical objective” whose spillovers nobody can predict, and fund work on doubling the size of an egg. “We want Wright’s law of eggs.” {089-J11}
## From start-up to bankruptcy
Next comes fierce competition. “Life for the firm should never be easy,” he said. Firms must be free to fail and people to land on their feet: bankruptcy is a healthy, normal part of life.
Then deep internationalisation, with more imports and exports, Indian multinationals and global firms operating without restriction. And immigration, so Indian firms can hire from all over the world.
~ Amit Varma added a caution. Nearly every monopoly, he said, comes about with the collusion of the state, so the government’s job, as far as possible, is a rule of law. {#collusion}

quote.text: The job of government is to create conditions where winning happens, where some great firms emerge with really high productivities.

side.boxText: Friedrich Hayek’s *The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism* names the error at the heart of the episode. A nation, Amit Varma said, is too complex for anyone to plan from the top, however enlightened the planner. {089-R01}

contQuote.text: What the government does is that it spends somebody else’s money on somebody else. And therefore the incentives drive you towards neither economizing nor towards seeking value. It is the worst way to spend money.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Of walled zones, waiting lists, a lost airline and a fined shopkeeper

stories.start: telling one story of one of the greatest industrial policy successes of world history
stories.end: The firms will surprise us in what they will do with the
stories.caption: SEEPZ, diamonds and software
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a walled zone in north Bombay
stories.head: Plan radios, get diamonds
body: In the 1970s, some bureaucrats looked at East Asia, which was making radios and electronic parts and exporting them all over the world, and asked why India could not do the same. Ajay Shah told what happened next as one of the greatest industrial-policy successes of world history.
Their diagnosis was customs duty. Import the transistors, pay 150 per cent duty, and a radio made in India would be far too expensive to re-export. {#duty}
So in the boondocks of north Bombay, they built a boundary wall around a chunk of land: the Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone, or SEEPZ. Every truck coming in and out was inspected.

Components came from the airport along special pathways, probably, Shah imagined, with somebody riding shotgun so that no transistor was smuggled into the Indian market. The finished radios went back to the planes in armoured trucks.
Then Indian firms saw what they had been given: freedom to import and to export. Through what Shah called “the organic process of discovery and not design”, two great industries emerged.

Entrepreneurs brought rough diamonds from South Africa and Antwerp, hired cheap Indian labour to polish them and sent them out again. India today polishes about 55 per cent of the world’s diamonds by number. {#diamonds}
~ Others imported computers, so that Indian programmers could build software for export. SEEPZ became one of the early sites of the Indian software industry.
stories.why: SEEPZ worked, Shah argued, because it added a pocket of freedom, not because anyone picked the right industry. Its two great winners were not on anyone’s list. Firms, he said, will surprise us with what they do with freedom. {089-S08}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s SEEPZ joke: the Allman Brothers Band played there and only Derek Trucks was examined, “because we were examining all the trucks.” {089-J12}

stories.start: And I want to share a little story here, and uh again
stories.end: where the you know, state still plays a really large role.
stories.caption: the wait for a telephone
stories.head: Seven years to say hello
body: About 70 per cent of Indians were born after liberalisation, Amit Varma said, so he feels it is his duty to keep retelling stories from before it. {#seventy}
He grew up in a privileged household; his father was a civil servant. Yet in the 1980s you waited seven or eight years for a telephone from the monopoly, MTNL. {#phonewait}

Flights cost about what they do now, he recalled, “except that eight thousand rupees then was a heck of a lot”. Even an officer’s family rarely flew, and he still remembers the excitement of his first flight.

~ When the sectors opened up in 1991, competitors flooded in and everything got cheaper. Television channels multiplied, and nobody needed to watch Doordarshan. The old monopolies simply stopped mattering. {089-S06}

quote.text: it’s not that they were shut down, it’s just that they became completely irrelevant.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah was less consoled: new public sector companies, he said, are still being created every year.

stories.start: It's heartbreaking thinking of the trajectory of Air India.
stories.end: Why does Lufthansa not run Bombay Delhi flights? Okay, and so on.
stories.caption: Air India’s long detour
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an airline’s round trip
stories.head: Tata to state and back again
body: Air India began as a private company owned by the Tatas, Ajay Shah said. The government expropriated it and made it a monopoly.

When the airline industry was opened to competition, Air India became a zombie firm, kept aloft only by taxpayers’ money. At its peak, Shah believed, it was bleeding 35,000 crore rupees a year in government subsidy. {#aibleed}
In what he called a great achievement of the BJP government, it was privatised and went back to the Tatas.

~ That is a good outcome, Shah said, but it leaves a question hanging: what if Air India had never been nationalised, and the industry had multiple global rivals all along? Why does Lufthansa not fly Bombay to Delhi? {089-S07}
stories.why: Privatisation recovers only part of the loss. The real cost is the decades of competition, service and growth that never happened while the state ran the airline.

stories.start: our friend Suyash has observed that the government chose UPI as the technology
stories.end: the use of coercive power, and we should watch out for it.
stories.caption: UPI and GPS
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on how technologies spread
stories.head: Pay by UPI, or pay a fine
body: The hosts’ friend Suyash, Ajay Shah said, had spotted something: the government chose UPI as the technology and then threw income tax law behind it. Inspectors can fine any shop that does not accept UPI.

Amit Varma admitted this was news to him. UPI is outstanding technology, he said, but every shopkeeper should be free to choose how to take payment, because that freedom is how the best payment systems emerge. {#upi}
Shah offered a contrast. In 1993, he thought, Bill Clinton signed off on releasing high-resolution GPS data to the whole world. {#clinton} People ran, not walked, to adopt it.
~ Nobody ordered every phone to carry GPS; phone makers longed for the day it would. India, Shah concluded, reaches for force too easily. {089-S05}

quote.text: So it is a very Indian malaise, the low trigger point for the use of coercive power
